title: JSON to JSON - Simple Mapping

explanation.whatHappened: Incoming JSON keys (snake_case) are mapped to canonical enterprise camelCase JSON format. Full name is created using string concatenation (++), and a nested invoice object is created.
explanation.functionDetails: Uses string concatenation (++), lower(), and now() as String {format: '...'} for core field remapping and data normalization.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you rename keys and concatenate strings while preserving data types in DataWeave?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Experience API to Process API transformation: standardizes client payloads into the enterprise canonical data model.

name: JSON to JSON - Simple Mapping

title: JSON to XML
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/xml
---
AccountRequest @(xmlns: "http://schemas.utility.com/account/v1", id: payload.account.id): {
  AccountName: payload.account.name,
  AccountTier: payload.account.tier,
  IsActive: payload.account.active
}

explanation.whatHappened: The incoming JSON object is transformed into a schema-compliant XML envelope with root XML attributes (@(xmlns: ..., id: ...)).
explanation.functionDetails: Uses 'output application/xml' and root attribute syntax '@(attr1: val, attr2: val)' to attach namespaces and attributes.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you add XML attributes and namespaces to the root tag in DataWeave 2.0?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Legacy SOAP Web Service integration (SAP, Mainframe, Oracle EBS) where REST JSON requests must be converted into SOAP XML payloads.

name: JSON to XML

title: XML to JSON
input:
<?xml version='1.0' encoding='UTF-8'?>
<GetCustomerResponse xmlns="http://utility.fpl.com/service">
  <Customer id="C-9912">
    <Name>Nextera Energy</Name>
    <MeterNumber>MTR-55410</MeterNumber>
    <Status>ACTIVE</Status>
    <CurrentReading unit="KWH">4820.75</CurrentReading>
  </Customer>
</GetCustomerResponse>
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
ns ns0 http://utility.fpl.com/service
---
{
  customerId: payload.ns0#GetCustomerResponse.ns0#Customer.@id,
  customerName: payload.ns0#GetCustomerResponse.ns0#Customer.ns0#Name,
  meterId: payload.ns0#GetCustomerResponse.ns0#Customer.ns0#MeterNumber,
  reading: payload.ns0#GetCustomerResponse.ns0#Customer.ns0#CurrentReading as Number,
  unit: payload.ns0#GetCustomerResponse.ns0#Customer.ns0#CurrentReading.@unit,
  status: payload.ns0#GetCustomerResponse.ns0#Customer.ns0#Status
}

explanation.whatHappened: The namespaced SOAP XML payload is parsed by extracting XML attributes (.@attr) and element text values into clean canonical JSON.
explanation.functionDetails: Uses namespace declarations ('ns ns0 http://...'), namespace element access ('ns0#Tag'), and attribute selectors ('.@id', '.@unit').
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you handle XML namespaces and attributes when parsing SOAP XML in DataWeave?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Converts SOAP System API responses into lightweight JSON payloads for Process and Experience APIs.

title: JSON to CSV
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/csv header=true, separator=","
---
payload map ((item) -> {
  "Employee ID": item.empId,
  "Full Name": upper(item.name),
  "Department": item.dept,
  "Annual Salary (USD)": item.salary
})
output:
"Employee ID","Full Name","Department","Annual Salary (USD)"
101,"NIRANJAN POTTER","Integration",145000
102,"AMIT SHARMA","Cloud",125000
103,"POOJA VERMA","Security",138000

explanation.whatHappened: The JSON array of objects is transformed into a structured CSV file with custom column headers and a comma delimiter.
explanation.functionDetails: Uses 'output application/csv header=true, separator=","' combined with map() to align each object property to a CSV column.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you generate a CSV file with custom header names and tab/pipe separators in DataWeave?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: SFTP file generation for nightly data warehouse exports, payroll feeds, and ERP flat-file ingestion.

name: JSON to CSV

title: CSV to JSON
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map ((row) -> {
  meterId: row.MeterID,
  readingDate: row.ReadingDate as Date {format: "yyyy-MM-dd"},
  kwh: row.ConsumptionKWH as Number,
  isActive: row.Status == "CONFIRMED"
})

explanation.whatHappened: Raw CSV rows are parsed and converted into a strongly typed JSON array with proper Number, Date, and Boolean types.
explanation.functionDetails: CSV fields default to String; explicit coercion ('as Number', 'as Date {format: "..."}', 'as Boolean') ensures type safety.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'CSV fields are always Strings. How do you convert CSV values to Numbers and Booleans safely?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Batch processing of inbound SFTP/File CSV drops before upserting records into databases or Salesforce.

name: CSV to JSON

title: Salesforce to Database Mapping
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  sfdc_account_id: payload.Id,
  company_name: payload.Name,
  account_type: if (payload.Type contains "Customer") "ACTIVE_CLIENT" else "PROSPECT",
  address_line1: payload.BillingStreet,
  city: payload.BillingCity,
  state_code: payload.BillingState,
  postal_code: payload.BillingPostalCode,
  revenue: payload.AnnualRevenue default 0,
  sync_timestamp: now() as String {format: "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS"}
}

explanation.whatHappened: A Salesforce Account SObject record is mapped to a relational SQL database table schema with conditional business rules and null defaults.
explanation.functionDetails: Uses conditional 'if (payload.Type contains "Customer") ... else ...' and the 'default' operator to prevent null insertion errors.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you handle conditionally computed fields and null fallbacks when syncing Salesforce to Postgres/Oracle?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Salesforce Change Data Capture (CDC) listener synchronizing real-time Account updates into an enterprise data warehouse.

name: Salesforce to Database Mapping

title: API Response Transformation

explanation.whatHappened: A raw backend API response is wrapped into an enterprise-standard API response envelope with status, correlationId, itemCount, and formatted totals.
explanation.functionDetails: Uses number formatting ('#,##0.00'), correlationId metadata, and sizeOf() to build a consistent response contract.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'What is your standard Experience API response wrapper pattern in MuleSoft?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Experience API layer delivering clean, predictable JSON envelopes to web portals and mobile applications.

name: API Response Transformation

title: Filter Array (where condition)
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload filter ($.active == true and $.role == "DEVELOPER" and $.rating >= 4.5)

explanation.whatHappened: Multiple boolean conditions are applied across array elements so only records matching all criteria are retained.
explanation.functionDetails: The filter() function evaluates a boolean predicate using '$' (current item) or explicit parameters ((item, index) -> ...).
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How does filter work in DataWeave, and what happens if no records match?' (Returns an empty array []).
explanation.realProjectUsage: Filtering active customer accounts, pending orders, or valid telemetry events from bulk payloads.

name: Filter Array (where condition)

title: Map Array - Add new field
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
var taxRate = 0.08
---
payload map ((item, index) -> item ++ {
  itemIndex: index + 1,
  taxAmount: item.basePrice * taxRate,
  finalPrice: item.basePrice * (1 + taxRate),
  isTaxable: item.category != "GROCERY"
})

explanation.whatHappened: Computed fields are appended to every object in the array while preserving all original keys using object concatenation (item ++ { ... }).
explanation.functionDetails: Object concatenation ('item ++ { key: value }') keeps existing keys intact; the index parameter tracks the 0-based position.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you add a new key to an existing object inside map without rewriting all existing keys?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Payload enrichment flows that attach audit timestamps, sequence IDs, or calculated tax fields to inbound records.

name: Map Array - Add new field

title: GroupBy - Group by Department
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload groupBy ((emp) -> emp.dept)

explanation.whatHappened: A flat array of employee records is grouped by department into a structured JSON object keyed by department name.
explanation.functionDetails: groupBy() returns an Object where each key is the grouping value and each value is an Array of matching elements.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'What is the return type of groupBy? Is it an Array or an Object?' (Always returns an Object).
explanation.realProjectUsage: Aggregating summary reports by customerId, grouping smart meter readings by deviceId, or bucketing transactions by date.

name: GroupBy - Group by Department

title: OrderBy - Sort by Salary
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
// Descending sort: minus (-) sign reverses order
payload orderBy -$.salary

explanation.whatHappened: The array of records is sorted by salary from highest to lowest (descending order).
explanation.functionDetails: orderBy() sorts ascending by default; prefixing a numeric expression with '-' (-$.salary) sorts in descending order.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you perform descending sorting in DataWeave without calling reverse()?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Ranking top accounts, prioritizing high-severity tickets, or ordering events from newest to oldest.

name: OrderBy - Sort by Salary

title: Distinct - Remove duplicates
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
import * from dw::core::Arrays
---
// distinctBy takes criteria key
payload distinctBy ((item) -> item.id)

explanation.whatHappened: Duplicate records are removed based on a unique business key (item.id), keeping only the first occurrence of each record.
explanation.functionDetails: distinctBy() evaluates a key expression per element and drops any subsequent items that produce a duplicate key.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'What is the difference between distinct and distinctBy in DataWeave?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Message deduplication for at-least-once queues (Anypoint MQ, SQS, Kafka) to guarantee idempotent downstream writes.

name: Distinct - Remove duplicates

title: Reduce - Sum of Salary
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  totalItems: sizeOf(payload),
  grandTotal: payload reduce ((line, acc = 0) -> acc + (line.qty * line.unitPrice)),
  currency: "USD"
}

explanation.whatHappened: All line items in the array are accumulated into a single grand total amount using a functional fold.
explanation.functionDetails: reduce() iterates with an item and accumulator: ((item, acc = 0) -> acc + item.amount).
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you calculate total order sum from a line-item array using reduce in DataWeave?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Invoice and billing pipelines computing line-item subtotals, tax totals, and order summaries.

name: Reduce - Sum of Salary

title: Flatten - Nested Array

explanation.whatHappened: A nested array of arrays ([['P-101', 'P-102'], ['P-201']]) is collapsed into a single one-dimensional array.
explanation.functionDetails: flatten() removes one level of array nesting, turning [[...], [...]] into a flat [...].
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'What does flatten() do and how is it different from flatMap()?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Combining results from Scatter-Gather routes or multiple database queries into a single unified array.

name: Flatten - Nested Array

title: Coalesce / Default - Handle Nulls
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  customerId: payload.customerId,
  displayName: payload.preferredName default payload.legalName default "Valued Customer",
  contactPhone: payload.billingPhone default payload.mobilePhone default "N/A",
  appliedDiscount: payload.discountRate default 0.05,
  hasPhone: (payload.billingPhone != null) or (payload.mobilePhone != null)
}

explanation.whatHappened: Optional or null fields are safely chained with fallback default values to eliminate NullPointerExceptions.
explanation.functionDetails: The 'default' keyword acts as a null-coalescing operator: if the left expression is null, the right fallback value is returned.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you prevent NullPointerExceptions in DataWeave when handling optional backend fields?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Defensive transformation pattern ensuring clean, non-null payloads are sent to strict downstream APIs and databases.

name: Coalesce / Default - Handle Nulls

title: Date Format - Change Date Format
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  standardIso: payload.isoTimestamp,
  usFormatted: (payload.isoTimestamp as DateTime) as String {format: "MM/dd/yyyy hh:mm a"},
  dateOnly: (payload.isoTimestamp as DateTime) as String {format: "yyyy-MM-dd"},
  timeOnly: (payload.isoTimestamp as DateTime) as String {format: "HH:mm:ss"},
  fromEpoch: (payload.epochSeconds as DateTime) as String {format: "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"},
  reparsedLegacy: (payload.legacyDate as Date {format: "dd/MM/yyyy"}) as String {format: "yyyy-MM-dd"}
}

explanation.whatHappened: Date values are converted seamlessly between ISO 8601, Unix Epoch timestamps, and custom regional date formats.
explanation.functionDetails: Uses native DateTime/Date coercion: '(val as DateTime) as String {format: "..."}'.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you parse a non-standard date string like dd/MM/yyyy into ISO yyyy-MM-dd in DataWeave?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: SAP and Mainframe integrations translating legacy regional date strings into modern ISO 8601 cloud timestamps.

name: Date Format - Change Date Format

title: String Functions - Upper, Lower, Concat
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
import * from dw::core::Strings
---
{
  fullName: capitalize(trim(payload.firstName)) ++ " " ++ capitalize(trim(payload.lastName)),
  upperCode: upper(payload.rawId),
  systemTag: (payload.rawId splitBy "-")[1],
  sequenceNum: (payload.rawId splitBy "-")[-1],
  isUrgent: payload.notes startsWith "urgent",
  notesSummary: substring(payload.notes, 8, 32),
  paddedId: leftPad("42", 6, "0")
}

explanation.whatHappened: Input strings are cleaned and formatted using whitespace trimming, capitalization, delimiter splitting, and left-padding.
explanation.functionDetails: Imports helpers from dw::core::Strings: capitalize(), trim(), leftPad(), startsWith(), and splitBy().
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you extract the last token from a hyphen-separated string?' ((str splitBy '-')[-1]).
explanation.realProjectUsage: Data cleansing, normalizing user input, and parsing structured tokens from correlation IDs.

name: String Functions - Upper, Lower, Concat

title: Type Coercion - String to Number
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  intNumber: payload.stringInt as Number,
  floatNumber: payload.stringFloat as Number,
  boolValue: payload.stringBool as Boolean,
  currencyString: "$" ++ (payload.numVal as String {format: "#,##0.00"}),
  parsedDate: payload.dateStr as Date,
  isPositive: (payload.stringFloat as Number) > 0
}

explanation.whatHappened: String inputs are strictly cast into native Number, Boolean, and Date data types using explicit type coercion.
explanation.functionDetails: Uses the 'as' keyword ('val as Number', 'val as Boolean', 'val as Date') to enforce schema types.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'What happens if you coerce an invalid string "ABC" as Number?' (Throws Cannot coerce String to Number).
explanation.realProjectUsage: Converting HTTP query parameters and headers (which arrive as Strings) into typed columns before database writes.

name: Type Coercion - String to Number

explanation.functionDetails: DataWeave match-case expressions replace deeply nested if-else ladders with clean, readable declarative rules.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'When should you use match-case instead of if-else in DataWeave?'

title: Lookup Function

explanation.functionDetails: Uses lookup(flowName, payload, timeout). Note: lookup() only invokes synchronous private flows without transactional boundaries.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'Can lookup() call an asynchronous flow or a flow with an HTTP listener?' (No, only private flows).

title: Pluck - Object to Array
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload pluck ((value, key, index) -> {
  regionCode: key as String,
  activeServers: value,
  sequence: index + 1
})

explanation.whatHappened: Key-value pairs of a JSON Object are iterated and converted into a structured Array of Objects.
explanation.functionDetails: pluck((value, key, index) -> ...) operates exclusively on Objects to emit an Array (the object counterpart to map()).
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you iterate over an Object instead of an Array in DataWeave?' (Use pluck()).
explanation.realProjectUsage: Transforming dynamic key-value maps or configuration caches into structured rows for UI tables and databases.

title: Merge Two Payloads

explanation.whatHappened: Two separate payloads (Customer and Billing) are merged into a single consolidated enterprise customer profile.
explanation.functionDetails: Object concatenation ('++') combines keys from both objects; if duplicate keys exist, the right-hand object takes precedence.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'What happens when you merge two objects with identical keys using ++ in DataWeave?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Scatter-Gather aggregation combining CRM (Salesforce) and Billing (SAP) responses into one canonical DTO.

name: Merge Two Payloads

title: SplitBy / JoinBy
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
import * from dw::core::Strings
---
{
  tagList: payload.tags splitBy ",",
  uppercaseTags: (payload.tags splitBy ",") map upper($),
  formattedPhone: payload.phoneSegments joinBy "-"
}

explanation.whatHappened: A comma-delimited string is split into an array using splitBy(), then recombined into a hyphenated string using joinBy().
explanation.functionDetails: splitBy(delimiter) returns an Array of Strings; joinBy(separator) joins an Array of Strings into a single String.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'How do you convert a comma-separated string into an array and back into a hyphenated string?'
explanation.realProjectUsage: Parsing comma-separated API query parameters (e.g., ?fields=id,name,email) and formatting SQL IN clauses.

name: SplitBy / JoinBy

title: Batch Job - DataWeave for Batch
script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
// Preparing payload inside Batch Aggregator for bulk commit
payload map ((record) -> {
  External_Id__c: record.id,
  Meter_Number__c: record.meter,
  KWH_Usage__c: record.kwh,
  Processed_Timestamp__c: now(),
  Batch_Source__c: "MULE_BATCH_STEP_2"
})

explanation.whatHappened: A Batch Aggregator chunk (e.g., 200 records) is transformed into Salesforce Bulk Upsert SObject format using an External ID.
explanation.functionDetails: Batch Aggregator collects records into an Array so DataWeave can map the entire batch for bulk database or Salesforce commits.
explanation.interviewQuestion: Interviewer asks: 'What is the payload structure inside a Batch Aggregator vs a Batch Step?' (Array vs single record).
explanation.realProjectUsage: Nightly batch synchronization of 100,000+ smart meter or customer records into Salesforce Bulk API 2.0.

name: Batch Job - DataWeave for Batch
